analysis.one_liner: Requires insurers to cover emergency care without prior authorization or out-of-network penalties.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 30 Senate sponsors to guarantee emergency-room coverage died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced health plans, insurers, Medicare Advantage plans, and Medicaid managed care plans to cover emergency services with no prior approval, even at out-of-network hospitals, and to judge emergencies by what a "prudent layperson" would think rather than by what a plan reviewer later decided. It also would have required coverage of care needed right after an emergency and limited extra charges for using an out-of-network emergency room. Introduced by Sen. Bob Graham with 29 cosponsors from both parties, it never received any committee action.
analysis.who_benefits: Insured people who end up in an emergency room — especially those whose insurer could otherwise deny the claim because they went out of network or because the plan later judged it wasn't an emergency. Emergency physicians and hospitals also benefit because the care they provide must be paid for.

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans to cover emergency services with no prior authorization, regardless of whether the provider is in the plan's network, and without regard to most other plan terms.

Defines an emergency by the 'prudent layperson' standard — whether an ordinary person with average knowledge of health could reasonably expect serious jeopardy without immediate care — instead of leaving the decision to the plan after the fact.

Requires coverage of maintenance and post-stabilization care after an emergency visit at an out-of-network hospital, with strict time limits: if the plan doesn't respond to an authorization request within 30 minutes, the care must be covered.

Caps cost-sharing: for emergency care under the listed exceptions, patients cannot be charged more for an out-of-network provider than an in-network one, and any higher emergency-room charges must be 'reasonable' under federal guidelines.
Extends the same protections to private plans serving Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries, including Medicare Advantage (section 1876) plans, Medicaid managed care, and Medicare Select policies.
Requires plans to educate members on what emergency coverage they have, when to use 911, what cost-sharing applies, and where in-network emergency departments are located.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care plans, which would have to pay for emergency and post-stabilization care they could previously deny or restrict. Employers who fund group plans would likely absorb much of that cost through premiums, and part of it would reach employees as premium contributions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employers funding plans

drawbacks.text: Plans that provide no emergency benefits at all are exempt, since the requirements apply only 'if a group health plan provides any benefits with respect to emergency services' — a plan could dodge the mandate by dropping emergency coverage.

Out-of-network protection is not automatic: plans may still deny or limit coverage for out-of-network emergency care except in three listed cases (circumstances beyond the patient's control, a prudent-layperson risk in going to an in-network hospital, or a physician referral).

The cost-sharing limits hinge on federal guidelines to be written later by three Cabinet secretaries after an advisory panel process, and the word 'reasonable' in the caps is undefined in the bill, leaving room for industry-favorable rules.
The mandate would raise costs for insurers and for employers who fund group plans, and some of that would flow back to workers as higher premiums — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core promise is real and aimed at one of the most feared denial practices of 1990s managed care — refusing to pay an emergency bill or charging huge out-of-network penalties. But the bill is weaker than it first appears: a plan could sidestep it by not covering emergency services, network restrictions still survive outside three exceptions, and the key limits are deferred to guidelines written later. The genuine cost is higher premiums spread across employers and employees, a fair trade for guaranteed emergency payment, though the vague "reasonable" standard invites the same disputes the bill was meant to end.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Graham introduced the bill on February 25, 1997, with original cosponsors Tim Hutchinson, Barbara Mikulski, and John Chafee.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
Twenty-nine senators cosponsored it — 20 Democrats and 9 Republicans.
That was the last recorded action: the Finance Committee never held a markup or scheduled the bill, and it died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

The protections it proposed — no prior authorization, the prudent layperson standard, out-of-network emergency coverage — were the leading patient-protection ideas of the late-1990s managed care debate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care plans kept their ability to deny or restrict payment for emergency care, including out-of-network charges, without any new federal obligation.

for.name: Bob Graham
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the Senate floor the day it was introduced.

for.name: 20 Senate Democrats and 9 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill 30 total sponsors across both parties.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair William Roth)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote; no action beyond referral is recorded.

against.name: Managed care and health insurance industry
against.role: Insurers and HMOs whose coverage practices the bill would regulate
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal mandates of this kind during the late-1990s managed care regulation debate.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan — 21 Democrats and 9 Republicans among the 30 sponsors — but no vote ever took place, so there is no roll-call record of where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill forces insurers to pay for emergency and post-stabilization care without prior authorization, including out-of-network care, and caps the extra charges they can impose for out-of-network emergency use. These were among the most profitable denial and penalty practices in managed care, so industry interest ran directly against patients.

industries.industry: Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care HMOs
industries.note: The bill extends the same emergency-coverage rules to private Medicare (section 1876) plans, Medicaid managed care contracts, and Medicare Select policies, ending their ability to restrict emergency care. Medicaid managed care contractors in particular were using network restrictions to steer patients away from emergency rooms.

Doctors and hospitals would be paid for emergency screening, stabilization, and post-stabilization care they currently sometimes provide unpaid, especially at out-of-network hospitals. Their interest in getting paid lines up with patients' interest in getting treated.

Employers who pay for group coverage would bear part of the added claims cost through premiums, but their employees gain guaranteed emergency protection. Many employer plans already offered emergency benefits, which triggers the mandate under the bill's own terms.
